item.title: A Second Try at Birthright Citizenship: Inside Trump's Narrower Orders After the Supreme Court Said No
item.body:
## A Setback, Then a Pivot

Earlier this year, the Supreme Court dealt a significant blow to one of the Trump administration's signature immigration priorities: a sweeping executive order that sought to end automatic citizenship for children born on U.S. soil to parents without legal status. The justices left intact the longstanding reading of the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause, which courts have interpreted for well over a century as guaranteeing citizenship to nearly everyone born within U.S. borders, regardless of their parents' immigration status.

Rather than abandon the effort, the White House appears to have recalibrated. According to administration officials, two new executive orders have been signed that narrow the scope dramatically, targeting categories of cases that officials argue sit closer to the edges of existing legal doctrine rather than challenging it head-on.

## What the New Orders Reportedly Do

The first order is said to focus on children born in the United States to parents identified as operatives of designated foreign terrorist organizations, as well as to accredited foreign diplomats — a group that has long been recognized, even under mainstream legal interpretations, as falling outside the scope of birthright citizenship because diplomats are considered to owe allegiance to their home government rather than U.S. jurisdiction.

The second order reportedly takes aim at so-called "birth tourism," the practice in which pregnant travelers enter the U.S. on tourist visas with the specific intent of giving birth on American soil so their child can obtain U.S. citizenship. Officials describe this as a narrower, more defensible target than a blanket policy change, since it deals with visa conditions and travel intent rather than attempting to redefine who is protected by the Constitution.

## Why the Narrower Approach

Legal analysts note that the strategy reflects lessons learned from the earlier court defeat. By focusing on diplomats, designated terrorist operatives, and visa-related conduct, the administration may be betting that these categories are less likely to trigger the same constitutional objections that sank the original, broader order. Some scholars point out that the "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" clause in the 14th Amendment has historically been read to exclude children of foreign diplomats, giving that piece of the new policy somewhat firmer legal footing than an outright reinterpretation of the amendment.

## Where Critics and Supporters Disagree

Immigrant rights advocates and several constitutional law scholars have voiced concern that even a narrower order could be used to expand executive authority over citizenship determinations — a power many legal experts argue rests with Congress and the courts, not the presidency. They also warn that "birth tourism" enforcement could create administrative hurdles or delays for pregnant travelers and new parents more broadly, even those with no intent to misuse visa rules.

Supporters of the orders counter that closing loopholes around diplomatic status and visa misuse is a targeted, common-sense step that does not require touching the core guarantee of birthright citizenship for the vast majority of people born in the U.S., including children of immigrants living and working in the country without legal status.

## What Happens Next

Legal challenges are widely expected, and courts will likely be asked to weigh in on whether these narrower orders can withstand scrutiny where the broader version could not. For now, the practical effect on hospitals, immigration attorneys, and prospective parents remains unclear, and officials have not detailed exactly how the new policies would be implemented or enforced.

As with the original order, the coming months will likely determine whether this second attempt marks a durable shift in immigration policy or another chapter in an ongoing legal standoff over the meaning of the 14th Amendment.
